HOSPITALITY — IDENTITY, DIGITAL

MARGATE, UK — 2026

Aster House

Twelve rooms on the Kent coast, booked direct.

YEAR
2026
SERVICES
Brand identity
Website & booking
Signage & print
CLIENT
Aster House, Margate
(OVERVIEW)

Aster House is a twelve-room hotel and dining room in a converted 1890s seed merchant’s in Margate. The owners came to us six months before opening with a name, a building and one commercial goal: fill the rooms without handing a cut of every stay to the booking platforms.

We designed the identity and the direct-booking website as one piece of work. The brand a guest finds on Instagram is the same one that takes the booking, sends the pre-arrival email, and greets them at the door.

The owners didn’t want the usual boutique-hotel look: no brass, no script logos, no stock lifestyle photography. Instead the system is built from limewash tones, one typeface, and photography shot in the building in afternoon light.

FIG. 01
THE SIGNWRITTEN LINTEL OVER THE FRONT DOOR, WHERE THE WORDMARK BEGAN.
FIG. 02 — KEY FOB, ROOM 7: LEATHER TAG, BRASS RING, THE HOUSE FIGURES
FIG. 03 — BREAKFAST CARD, FILLED IN AT TURNDOWN AND HUNG ON THE DOOR

A hotel brand lives at check-in, not on the homepage.

FIG. 04 — ROOM 4, NUMBERED BY THE SAME SIGNWRITER AS THE LINTEL
FIG. 05 — STAIR HALL TO ROOMS 1–6

(IDENTITY)

A wordmark painted on the lintel, then redrawn for screen.

The signwriter’s lettering over the front door became a single-weight logotype that also works at favicon size. Room numbers, key fobs, the breakfast card and the bill all use the same figures, so the signage does the job of the brand.

Guest stationery is printed by a local press in two colours, so reprints stay cheap enough for a twelve-room hotel.

(DIRECT BOOKING)

The old site sent guests to a third-party booking widget. We replaced it with a short booking flow on the hotel’s own site: dates, room, a note to the house, payment. The full price, including taxes, shows from the first screen, and there are no upsell steps.

Every room has its own page with real photographs, the bed size, the view and what can be heard from it at night. Rates, the seasonal dinner menu and photography are all managed by the owners in a headless CMS. The confirmation, pre-arrival and post-stay emails use the same type and tone of voice as the site.

CULTURE — ART DIRECTION

LONDON — 2026

Nocturne

Three nights of music, lit by a single source.

YEAR
2026
SERVICES
Art direction
Campaign
Photography direction
CLIENT
Nocturne Festival
(OVERVIEW)

Nocturne is a winter music festival held across three nights in February, in buildings that are usually closed after dark: a library, a swimming baths, a disused print hall. The festival needed a campaign that sold the setting before the line-up was announced.

We wrote one rule for every image: a single light source and nothing else. It applied to the posters, the photography in each venue, the trailer and the stage lighting brief, so the festival looks the same in a tube station as it does on the night.

The palette is deep blue and near-black, with no colour coding by day or venue. Typography is kept to one size on the posters, so the light does the shouting.

FIG. 01
THE BATHS, NIGHT TWO. SHOT FROM THE DEEP END WITH THE HOUSE LIGHTS OFF.
FIG. 02 — LIBRARY READING ROOM, SINGLE FOLLOW-SPOT
FIG. 03 — PRINT HALL STAGE, FLUORESCENT TUBES ONLY

If it can be seen in daylight, it isn’t Nocturne.

(CAMPAIGN)

Posters that switch between day and night.

Each poster runs in two versions: ink on white for daytime sites, white on deep blue for late-night and underground sites. The vertical light bar sits in the same position in both, so a run of mixed posters still reads as one campaign.

Dates and venue are the only text. Tickets are sold through a short URL rather than a QR code.

(ROLLOUT)

The campaign ran in three waves: venues first, then the trailer, then the line-up. Each wave reused the same photographs with more information added, so early posters didn’t go out of date.

ARCHITECTURE — DIGITAL

LONDON — 2025

Forma

A practice website that reads like a monograph.

YEAR
2025
SERVICES
Website
Digital design
Development
CLIENT
Forma Architects
(OVERVIEW)

Forma is a fourteen-person architecture practice working on housing, schools and public buildings. Its portfolio lived in a 60-page PDF that was out of date the day it was sent. We replaced it with a website the practice can keep current itself.

The audience is narrow: clients writing tender shortlists, planning officers, and architects deciding where to apply. Each needs to find comparable buildings quickly, so the site is organised around projects, not around the practice.

There is no animation on the drawings and no carousel on the homepage. The pages are built like the practice’s printed monographs: wide margins, captions in the margin, and drawings given the same space as photographs.

FIG. 01 — BRISE-SOLEIL, HOLLIS ROAD SCHOOL
FIG. 02 — COMPETITION MODEL, PHOTOGRAPHED FOR THE PROJECT PAGE
(STRUCTURE)

Every project is entered once in the CMS with its sector, location, stage, size and status. The index can then be filtered by any of them, so a council looking for completed schools under 5,000 m² finds them in two clicks.

Project pages are assembled from the same set of modules as this case study. The practice adds a building by uploading photographs and drawings and choosing a layout for each, with no design or development time needed.

(DRAWINGS)

Plans you can read at any size.

Drawings are uploaded as vector files, so they stay sharp when zoomed and load faster than the old JPEG exports. Each plan carries its scale and floor in a caption, never inside the image.

Drawings deserve the same space as photographs.

SPORT — IDENTITY

BRISTOL, UK — 2025

Arc Athletics

A running club identity drawn from the 400-metre lap.

YEAR
2025
SERVICES
Brand identity
Kit design
Signage
CLIENT
Arc Athletics
(OVERVIEW)

Arc is a members’ running club that trains on a council athletics track in Bristol: road runners, track sessions on Tuesday and Thursday, and a junior squad on Saturdays. It had grown from a WhatsApp group to [X] members and needed to look like a club, not a training app.

Most running brands borrow the language of speed: slanted type, gradients, lightning. The club wanted the opposite, something that would sit comfortably on a 10-year-old’s first vest and on a masters runner’s race number.

Everything in the identity is taken from the track itself: the curve of the bend, the white lane lines, the numbered lanes and the clay colour of the surface.

FIG. 01 — CLUB VEST. THE ARC DOUBLES AS THE RACE-NUMBER FRAME.
FIG. 02 — THE MARK: LANES 1 AND 2 OF THE BEND, DRAWN TO SCALE

Every mark comes from the track.

FIG. 03
LANE NUMERALS BECAME THE CLUB’S FIGURES FOR KIT, SESSION BOARDS AND RESULTS.

(SYSTEM)

Two colours, one curve, eight numerals.

The identity runs on clay and cream, with ink for type. The arc can be cropped, repeated or used as a frame, but never rotated. That keeps it recognisable on a vest at 50 metres and on a phone at 2cm.

Session plans, results and race-entry posts use one shared template, so volunteer coaches can publish in the club style without design software.

FIG. 04 — THURSDAY NIGHT SESSION. SIGNAGE WAS TESTED UNDER FLOODLIGHTS, NOT IN THE STUDIO.
(KIT & SIGNAGE)

Kit is made by a UK supplier in a single colourway, with the arc printed in one colour, which keeps the minimum order low enough for a volunteer-run club. Juniors get the same vest as seniors.

Track-side boards for start lines, warm-up areas and the club hut are printed on composite panel and use the same lane numerals as the kit.

Outcome: membership grew from [X] to [Y] in the first season after launch.

The juniors ask for the vest before they ask about the sessions.

(OVERVIEW)

Halden is an independent journal about landscape and how land is used: farming, rewilding, planning, walking. It is published twice a year by a small team of writers and ecologists. We designed the first issue and the format every issue after it will follow.

The editors wanted a magazine that could carry long reporting and long photo essays without either one feeling like filler. The answer was a strict rhythm: text sections and picture sections alternate, and they never share a spread.

Every photo essay is commissioned, not licensed. We briefed photographers to shoot in flat, overcast light, so the colour of the land carries the pages rather than dramatic skies.

(FORMAT)

Each issue runs to 192 pages at 230 × 300 mm, printed on an uncoated stock that holds the greens without making them glossy. The cover is a single photograph with the masthead set small at the foot.

The grid has two columns of text and one wide margin for notes, maps and sources. Long reads can carry footnotes without breaking the reading line, which mattered to writers coming from academic and policy backgrounds.

(TYPOGRAPHY)

One serif for reading, one sans for the margins.

Body text is set at 10.5 pt for long reading. Notes, maps and data use a sans at a single small size, so readers can tell at a glance what is story and what is reference.

It’s the first magazine our contributors keep on the shelf rather than in the recycling.

(OVERVIEW)

Aster House is a twelve-room hotel and dining room in a converted 1890s seed merchant’s in Margate. The owners came to us six months before opening with a name, a building and one commercial goal: fill the rooms without handing a cut of every stay to the booking platforms.

We designed the identity and the direct-booking website as one piece of work. The brand a guest finds on Instagram is the same one that takes the booking, sends the pre-arrival email, and greets them at the door.

The owners didn’t want the usual boutique-hotel look: no brass, no script logos, no stock lifestyle photography. Instead the system is built from limewash tones, one typeface, and photography shot in the building in afternoon light.

FIG. 01
THE SIGNWRITTEN LINTEL OVER THE FRONT DOOR, WHERE THE WORDMARK BEGAN.
FIG. 02 — KEY FOB, ROOM 7: LEATHER TAG, BRASS RING, THE HOUSE FIGURES
FIG. 03 — BREAKFAST CARD, FILLED IN AT TURNDOWN AND HUNG ON THE DOOR

A hotel brand lives at check-in, not on the homepage.

FIG. 04 — ROOM 4, NUMBERED BY THE SAME SIGNWRITER AS THE LINTEL
FIG. 05 — STAIR HALL TO ROOMS 1–6

(IDENTITY)

A wordmark painted on the lintel, then redrawn for screen.

The signwriter’s lettering over the front door became a single-weight logotype that also works at favicon size. Room numbers, key fobs, the breakfast card and the bill all use the same figures, so the signage does the job of the brand.

Guest stationery is printed by a local press in two colours, so reprints stay cheap enough for a twelve-room hotel.

(DIRECT BOOKING)

The old site sent guests to a third-party booking widget. We replaced it with a short booking flow on the hotel’s own site: dates, room, a note to the house, payment. The full price, including taxes, shows from the first screen, and there are no upsell steps.

Every room has its own page with real photographs, the bed size, the view and what can be heard from it at night. Rates, the seasonal dinner menu and photography are all managed by the owners in a headless CMS. The confirmation, pre-arrival and post-stay emails use the same type and tone of voice as the site.

(OVERVIEW)

Nocturne is a winter music festival held across three nights in February, in buildings that are usually closed after dark: a library, a swimming baths, a disused print hall. The festival needed a campaign that sold the setting before the line-up was announced.

We wrote one rule for every image: a single light source and nothing else. It applied to the posters, the photography in each venue, the trailer and the stage lighting brief, so the festival looks the same in a tube station as it does on the night.

The palette is deep blue and near-black, with no colour coding by day or venue. Typography is kept to one size on the posters, so the light does the shouting.

Arc Athletics

A running club identity drawn from the 400-metre lap.

YEAR
2025
SERVICES
Brand identity
Kit design
Signage
CLIENT
Arc Athletics
(OVERVIEW)

Arc is a members’ running club that trains on a council athletics track in Bristol: road runners, track sessions on Tuesday and Thursday, and a junior squad on Saturdays. It had grown from a WhatsApp group to [X] members and needed to look like a club, not a training app.

Most running brands borrow the language of speed: slanted type, gradients, lightning. The club wanted the opposite, something that would sit comfortably on a 10-year-old’s first vest and on a masters runner’s race number.

Everything in the identity is taken from the track itself: the curve of the bend, the white lane lines, the numbered lanes and the clay colour of the surface.

FIG. 01 — CLUB VEST. THE ARC DOUBLES AS THE RACE-NUMBER FRAME.
FIG. 02 — THE MARK: LANES 1 AND 2 OF THE BEND, DRAWN TO SCALE

Every mark comes from the track.

FIG. 03
LANE NUMERALS BECAME THE CLUB’S FIGURES FOR KIT, SESSION BOARDS AND RESULTS.

(SYSTEM)

Two colours, one curve, eight numerals.

A journal about land, paced like a walk.

Halden Journal
(OVERVIEW)

Halden is an independent journal about landscape and how land is used: farming, rewilding, planning, walking. It is published twice a year by a small team of writers and ecologists. We designed the first issue and the format every issue after it will follow.

The editors wanted a magazine that could carry long reporting and long photo essays without either one feeling like filler. The answer was a strict rhythm: text sections and picture sections alternate, and they never share a spread.

Every photo essay is commissioned, not licensed. We briefed photographers to shoot in flat, overcast light, so the colour of the land carries the pages rather than dramatic skies.

FIG. 01 — ISSUE 1, “THE LONG VIEW”. THE ONLY SPREAD WHERE IMAGE AND TEXT MEET.
FIG. 02 — PHOTO ESSAY: A HAY MEADOW LEFT UNCUT FOR ONE YEAR
FIG. 03 — PHOTO ESSAY: FIELD CLEARANCE ON AN UPLAND FARM

FIG. 04
PICTURE SECTIONS RUN FULL-BLEED ACROSS THE GUTTER WITH NO CAPTIONS ON THE PAGE. CAPTIONS ARE COLLECTED AT THE END OF EACH ESSAY.
(FORMAT)

Each issue runs to 192 pages at 230 × 300 mm, printed on an uncoated stock that holds the greens without making them glossy. The cover is a single photograph with the masthead set small at the foot.

The grid has two columns of text and one wide margin for notes, maps and sources. Long reads can carry footnotes without breaking the reading line, which mattered to writers coming from academic and policy backgrounds.

(TYPOGRAPHY)

One serif for reading, one sans for the margins.

Body text is set at 10.5 pt for long reading. Notes, maps and data use a sans at a single small size, so readers can tell at a glance what is story and what is reference.

It’s the first magazine our contributors keep on the shelf rather than in the recycling.

Design exhibitions often assume visitors already know the field. The curators wanted a show that someone who came in to shelter from the rain could follow, so every decision started with the label rather than the poster.

The identity is built from three solid shapes in the depot’s original paint colours. They mark the three sections of the show, each with its own colour, on the walls, in the catalogue and on the tickets.

FIG. 01 — SECTION TWO, “OBJECTS”. PLINTH LABELS SIT AT SEATED EYE LEVEL.
FIG. 02 — SECTION ONE, “ROOMS”. WALL TEXT IS NEVER MORE THAN 60 WORDS.

Write labels for the visitor, not the lender.

(CATALOGUE)

A catalogue that works as a guide on the day.

The 96-page catalogue follows the route through the depot, room by room, and fits in a coat pocket. Each work has one photograph, one paragraph from the maker and the label number used on the wall, so the book and the room can be read together.

FIG. 03 — CAMPAIGN POSTER. THE SHAPES STAND IN FOR THE THREE SECTIONS.
FIG. 04 — THE DEPOT BEFORE INSTALL, USED FOR THE FIRST TEASER
(LABELS & WAYFINDING)

Labels are set large enough to read without stepping over the barrier line, and each one answers the same three questions in the same order: who made it, what it’s made of, and why it’s here. Large-print and audio versions use the same numbering.

The route is marked on the floor in the colour of each section, so visitors know where they are without reading a map.

Outcome: [X] visitors over ten weeks, with the catalogue reprinted in week [Y].

The comments book was full of people saying they didn’t think design was for them, until now.
